summary.text: Take the composite number \(N=23492890653051=3\cdot37\cdot43\cdot42307\cdot116341\), whose displayed factors are distinct primes. Multiplicativity of the gcd-sum and the identity \(\sum_{k=1}^{p}\gcd(k,p)=2p-1\) for primes give \(\sum_{k=1}^{N}\gcd(k,N)=610815156979325\), so adding 1 yields \(26N\) and therefore \(a(N)=1\).

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
S(n)=\sum_{k=1}^{n}\gcd(k,n),
\qquad
a(n)=\frac{n}{\gcd(n,1+S(n))}.
\]
We will exhibit the composite integer
\[
N=23492890653051
\]
for which \(a(N)=1\). This directly disproves the asserted equivalence.

We first establish the formula that will make the otherwise enormous sum \(S(N)\) manageable.

For a positive integer \(n\), group the integers \(k\in\{1,\ldots,n\}\) according to the value \(d=\gcd(k,n)\). Necessarily \(d\mid n\). Write \(n=dq\). The condition \(\gcd(k,n)=d\) is equivalent to writing \(k=dj\), where \(1\leq j\leq q\) and \(\gcd(j,q)=1\), because
\[
\gcd(dj,dq)=d\gcd(j,q).
\]
Thus there are exactly \(\varphi(q)=\varphi(n/d)\) integers \(k\) in this group, and every one contributes \(d\) to the gcd sum. Consequently
\[
S(n)=\sum_{d\mid n}d\,\varphi(n/d). \tag{1}
\]

In particular, suppose that \(n=p_1p_2\cdots p_r\) is a product of distinct primes. Every divisor \(d\) corresponds to a subset \(I\subseteq\{1,\ldots,r\}\), with
\[
d=\prod_{i\in I}p_i,
\qquad
\frac nd=\prod_{i\notin I}p_i.
\]
For a product of distinct primes, Euler's totient formula gives
\[
\varphi(n/d)=\prod_{i\notin I}(p_i-1).
\]
This formula follows directly from the Chinese remainder theorem: a residue class modulo the product is coprime to that product exactly when its component modulo every prime factor is nonzero, and there are \(p_i-1\) nonzero choices modulo \(p_i\). Substituting in (1) gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
S(n)
 &=\sum_{I\subseteq\{1,\ldots,r\}}
   \left(\prod_{i\in I}p_i\right)
   \left(\prod_{i\notin I}(p_i-1)\right)\\
 &=\prod_{i=1}^r\bigl(p_i+(p_i-1)\bigr)
 =\prod_{i=1}^r(2p_i-1). \tag{2}
\end{aligned}
\]
The second equality is simply the expansion of the product: for each index \(i\), choosing the term \(p_i\) places \(i\) in \(I\), while choosing \(p_i-1\) leaves it outside \(I\).

We now factor the proposed counterexample:
\[
N=3\cdot37\cdot43\cdot42307\cdot116341. \tag{3}
\]
For completeness, the successive products are
\[
3\cdot37=111,
\quad111\cdot43=4773,
\quad4773\cdot42307=201931311,
\]
and
\[
201931311\cdot116341=23492890653051.
\]
All five factors in (3) are distinct primes. The primality of \(3,37,43\) follows immediately by trial division by primes not exceeding their square roots. We include explicit compact checks for the two larger factors.

We use the following elementary Lucas primality criterion. Let \(m>1\), suppose the complete prime factorization of \(m-1\) is known, and suppose there is an integer \(b\) such that
\[
b^{m-1}\equiv1\pmod m
\]
and, for every prime \(q\mid m-1\),
\[
\gcd\bigl(b^{(m-1)/q}-1,m\bigr)=1. \tag{4}
\]
Then \(m\) is prime.

Indeed, let \(r\) be any prime divisor of \(m\), and let \(t\) be the multiplicative order of \(b\) modulo \(r\). The first congruence implies \(t\mid m-1\). For every prime \(q\mid m-1\), condition (4) implies that
\(b^{(m-1)/q}\not\equiv1\pmod r\), so \(t\nmid(m-1)/q\). If \(q^e\) is the exact power of \(q\) dividing \(m-1\), this forces \(q^e\mid t\). Applying this to every prime divisor \(q\) of \(m-1\) shows that \(m-1\mid t\). Hence \(t=m-1\). On the other hand, the multiplicative order modulo the prime \(r\) divides \(r-1\), so \(m-1\mid r-1\). Therefore \(r\geq m\). Since \(r\mid m\), we also have \(r\leq m\), and hence \(r=m\). Thus \(m\) itself is prime.

For \(m=42307\),
\[
m-1=42306=2\cdot3\cdot11\cdot641.
\]
The number \(641\) is prime: its square root is less than \(26\), and division by the primes
\(2,3,5,7,11,13,17,19,23\) gives nonzero remainders (respectively \(1,2,1,4,3,4,12,14,20\)). Thus the displayed factorization of \(42306\) is a complete prime factorization. Take \(b=3\). Repeated squaring modulo \(42307\) gives
\[
3^{42306}\equiv1\pmod{42307},
\]
and, for the prime divisors \(q=2,3,11,641\) of \(42306\), gives the following residues:
\[
\begin{array}{c|c}
q&3^{42306/q}\pmod{42307}\\ \hline
2&42306\\
3&36715\\
11&17937\\
641&10961
\end{array}
\]
Applying the Euclidean algorithm to each residue minus one and \(42307\) gives
\[
\gcd(42305,42307)=
\gcd(36714,42307)=
\gcd(17936,42307)=
\gcd(10960,42307)=1.
\]
The criterion therefore proves that \(42307\) is prime.

Similarly, for \(m=116341\),
\[
m-1=116340=2^2\cdot3\cdot5\cdot7\cdot277.
\]
The number \(277\) is prime: its square root is less than \(17\), and its remainders upon division by \(2,3,5,7,11,13\) are respectively \(1,1,2,4,2,4\), all nonzero. Take \(b=14\). Modular exponentiation gives
\[
14^{116340}\equiv1\pmod{116341},
\]
and the calculations for the distinct prime divisors of \(116340\) are
\[
\begin{array}{c|c}
q&14^{116340/q}\pmod{116341}\\ \hline
2&116340\\
3&50801\\
5&81650\\
7&10889\\
277&35125
\end{array}
\]
The corresponding Euclidean-algorithm computations are
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\gcd(116339,116341)=1,\\
&\gcd(50800,116341)=1,\\
&\gcd(81649,116341)=1,\\
&\gcd(10888,116341)=1,\\
&\gcd(35124,116341)=1.
\end{aligned}
\]
The criterion proves that \(116341\) is prime. Hence (3) is indeed a product of five distinct primes, and formula (2) applies.

Using (2), we now evaluate the gcd sum without summing billions of individual terms:
\[
\begin{aligned}
S(N)
&=(2\cdot3-1)(2\cdot37-1)(2\cdot43-1)
  (2\cdot42307-1)(2\cdot116341-1)\\
&=5\cdot73\cdot85\cdot84613\cdot232681.
\end{aligned}
\]
The successive products are
\[
5\cdot73=365,
\qquad365\cdot85=31025,
\]
\[
31025\cdot84613=2625118325,
\]
and finally
\[
2625118325\cdot232681=610815156979325.
\]
Therefore
\[
S(N)=610815156979325.
\]
Adding one yields the crucial divisibility relation
\[
1+S(N)=610815156979326
       =26\cdot23492890653051
       =26N. \tag{5}
\]
It follows from (5) that \(N\mid 1+S(N)\), and therefore
\[
\gcd(N,1+S(N))=N.
\]
Since \(N>0\), we conclude that
\[
a(N)=\frac{N}{\gcd(N,1+S(N))}=\frac NN=1. \tag{6}
\]

However, \(N\neq1\), and \(N\) is not prime: equation (3) shows in particular that
\[
N=3\cdot7830963551017,
\]
where both factors are greater than \(1\). Thus for this \(N\), the left side of the conjectured equivalence, \(a(N)=1\), is true by (6), while the right side, “\(N=1\) or \(N\) is prime,” is false. Hence it is not true that for every positive integer \(n\), \(a(n)=1\) if and only if \(n=1\) or \(n\) is prime.
